concept.name: Endowment effect
concept.definition: The finding that people value a good more highly once they own it: the minimum they will accept to give it up substantially exceeds the maximum they would pay to acquire it. Named by Thaler (1980) and demonstrated experimentally by Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler (1990), it is commonly explained by loss aversion around an ownership reference point.
concept.intuition: The moment a position is in your account, it feels worth more than the identical position you do not own.
concept.mechanics: Ownership shifts the reference point so that selling is coded as a loss; in the classic Cornell mug experiments, sellers demanded roughly twice what buyers offered. Competing explanations include psychological ownership, reference-price asymmetries, and experimental artifacts (Plott and Zeiler).
concept.failure_modes: The effect weakens for experienced traders of a good, for goods with close substitutes, and under some experimental designs, and its interpretation as pure loss aversion is disputed. It cannot justify holding a position against contrary evidence.
concept.misconceptions: It is not mere sentimental attachment - it appears within minutes of randomly assigned ownership. Nor does it prove markets are irrational: induced-value markets in the same experiments cleared efficiently.
concept.example: An investor refuses to sell a stock at $80 even though, if she did not already own it, she would not pay more than $60 for it today.
